newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Lobbyists call on Botswana to delay media controls.
newsitem.headline: Lobbyists call on Botswana to delay media controls.

text.p: The Paris-based lobby group Reporters Sans Frontieres appealed to Botswana's President Ketumile Masire on Thursday to delay a law proposing new controls on the country's media.
The law would oblige journalists to join a press council and impose restrictions on the ownership of publications.
Botswana's cabinet is due to consider the bill on July 9 before sending it to parliament for debate on August 15.
Reporters Sans Frontieres said in an open letter to Masire it was worried that the draft law included "restrictive measures towards the national and international press".
The Mass Media Communications bill provides for a broadcasting board and press council which would regulate media in the southern African country.
The law would force reporters and editors to join the council, which would be directed by five government officials, five government-appointed members of the public and six journalists.

The council would be empowered to impose fines on journalists and publishers of up to 1,000 pula ($280) or a year in jail for, among other things, failing to register a publication or reporting without government accreditation.
The average income for a journalist in Botswana is around $700 per month.
The law would also limit foreign stakes in local publications to a maximum of 20 percent.
Reporters Sans Frontieres General Secretary Robert Menard appealed to Masire to discuss the proposals with interested parties before proceeding.

"We ask you to promote a voluntary media-driven council instead of one including government-appointed people. Moreover we remind you that any legislation affecting the media must guarantee the right to free speech and media freedom," he said.
He reminded Masire that the United Nations Commission of Human Rights considered "detention as punishment for the peaceful expression of an opinion" as a violation of human rights.
"Therefore, we urge you to cancel all plans to give journalists prison sentences because of their job," Menard said.
The Namibia-based Media Institute of Southern Africa has also called for a delay in passing the bill.
